latent_mechanisms.display_name: Intravascular proliferation of malignant large B cells
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Selective growth of CD20+ large B-lymphoma cells confined to lumina of capillaries, post-capillary venules, and small arteries across multiple organs without forming nodal/parenchymal masses; defines IVLBCL.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Defective tumor cell homing/extravasation (loss of CD29/CD54)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Down-regulation of β1 integrin (CD29) and ICAM-1 (CD54) on tumor cells impairs transendothelial migration, producing the pathognomonic intravascular trapping phenotype rather than nodal disease.

Tumor plugs in small vessels obstruct perfusion, producing patchy, multifocal organ ischemia (CNS infarcts, pulmonary microvascular dysfunction, AKI, adrenal infarction) that drives much of IVLBCL morbidity independent of bulk tumor.

Involvement of cerebral microvasculature producing encephalopathy, multifocal stroke-like deficits, cognitive decline, dementia-like syndromes, seizures, and progressive neurologic decline; very common in classical (non-Asian) variant and a major cause of CNS relapse.

Skin microvessel involvement producing erythematous patches, plaques, telangiectasia-like lesions, indurated nodules, peau d'orange, and panniculitis-like findings, predominantly on lower extremities/abdomen; cutaneous-only variant has female predominance and better prognosis.

Tumor cells lodge in alveolar capillaries causing progressive dyspnea, hypoxemia, ground-glass/diffuse interstitial pattern that mimics interstitial pneumonia, PE, or CTEPH; perfusion defects often outpace radiographic findings; can progress to ARDS.
Glomerular capillary and peritubular vessel involvement causing AKI, subnephrotic proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria; biopsy may show intracapillary atypical lymphocytes.

Frequent (especially Asian variant) bilateral adrenal involvement producing adrenal enlargement on imaging and primary adrenal insufficiency; a recognized cause of unexplained hyponatremia, hypotension, and adrenal crisis in IVLBCL.

Intrasinusoidal/intravascular tumor infiltration of marrow seen frequently in Asian (hemophagocytic) variant; produces cytopenias and provides the highest-yield random biopsy site for diagnosis; correlates with secondary HLH risk.

Liver and splenic sinusoidal involvement producing hepatosplenomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, transaminase elevation, and contributing to HLH-like cytokine and reticuloendothelial activation; especially prominent in Asian variant.

Macrophage activation/cytokine storm precipitated by widespread intravascular lymphoma, fulfilling HLH-2004 criteria; characteristic of the Asian/hemophagocytic variant and a major early-mortality driver via DIC, multi-organ failure, and hepatic dysfunction.

Tumor-derived and macrophage-derived cytokine release producing fever of unknown origin, drenching sweats, fatigue, and weight loss—often the only early presenting feature for many months before diagnosis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Tumor lysis metabolic burden after chemotherapy initiation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Following R-CHOP induction, the high cell-turnover lymphoma burden releases urate, K+, phosphate, and LDH within 24–72 h, predisposing to AKI, hyperkalemia, and arrhythmia; risk modulated by tumor burden, baseline LDH, and renal function.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Diagnostic delay due to occult, multisystem presentation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Antemortem diagnosis is notoriously difficult: presentations as FUO, dementia, or multi-organ dysfunction without lymphadenopathy or mass lesion; many cases historically diagnosed at autopsy. Drives accumulated organ injury before treatment.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Loss of β1 integrin and ICAM-1 prevents extravasation, so clonal B cells accumulate within vessel lumens—this is the defining mechanism that creates the intravascular phenotype rather than nodal DLBCL.
Tumor cell plugs progressively obstruct capillary/venule lumens, producing multifocal small-vessel ischemia that explains organ-specific dysfunction patterns out of proportion to bulk disease.
Cerebral and leptomeningeal microvasculature are predilection sites; CNS involvement is reported in 30–40% of classical IVLBCL and is a frequent cause of relapse even after systemic CR.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: predominant in cutaneous-only Western variant (female predominance, better prognosis)
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Dermal vessel involvement produces telangiectasia, plaques, painful nodules, and peau d'orange that are diagnostically high-yield for biopsy and define the cutaneous variant.
Alveolar capillary plugging produces hypoxemia and dyspnea often exceeding radiographic findings; pulmonary involvement is frequent and may mimic PE/CTEPH/ILD.
Glomerular and peritubular capillary involvement produces AKI and proteinuria; renal biopsy showing intracapillary atypical lymphocytes can be the diagnostic finding.
Bilateral adrenal infiltration is one of the most characteristic IVLBCL findings and produces primary adrenal insufficiency that contributes to hypotension and unexplained hyponatremia.
Intrasinusoidal marrow infiltration drives cytopenias, contributes to HLH biology, and is the highest-yield random biopsy site for antemortem diagnosis in the Asian variant.
Hepatic and splenic sinusoidal infiltration explains hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis, and cholestatic dysfunction that frequently dominate the Asian variant phenotype.
Marrow and hepatosplenic infiltration triggers macrophage activation/IFN-γ–driven HLH biology, the defining systemic complication of the Asian/hemophagocytic IVLBCL variant.
Reticuloendothelial activation in liver and spleen amplifies cytokine output (IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-18) characteristic of secondary HLH in IVLBCL.
Tumor-cell and reactive cytokine release produces FUO, drenching sweats, weight loss—frequently the only initial clue and the reason IVLBCL is on the FUO differential.
Generic lymphoma tumor burden is mechanistically equivalent to the intravascular proliferation in IVLBCL and drives downstream LDH/sIL-2R/β2-microglobulin axes.
LDH is markedly elevated (often 2–10× ULN) in IVLBCL due to high tumor turnover and microvascular ischemia; one of the most reliable laboratory clues in occult presentations.
Multifocal tissue ischemia from microvascular plugging contributes additively to LDH elevation beyond tumor turnover alone, partly explaining the very high LDH levels observed.
Ratio-form LDH (LDH/ULN) is used in IPI scoring; in IVLBCL ratios of 2–10 are typical and correlate with tumor burden and prognosis.
sIL-2R is markedly elevated in IVLBCL (frequently >5,000 U/mL) reflecting both tumor burden and reactive lymphocyte/macrophage activation; useful biomarker in Japan for diagnosis and follow-up.
HLH biology further amplifies sIL-2R, often producing the highest sIL-2R values seen clinically; helps distinguish HLH-overlap IVLBCL from indolent presentations.
β2-microglobulin reflects tumor cell turnover and is commonly elevated in IVLBCL, with prognostic value.
Macrophage activation in IVLBCL-associated HLH produces marked hyperferritinemia (often >2,000–10,000 ng/mL); a useful flag in unexplained febrile cytopenias.
TNF-α–mediated suppression of lipoprotein lipase produces hypertriglyceridemia, an HLH-2004 criterion frequently positive in Asian-variant IVLBCL.
Hyperfibrinolysis and consumption produce hypofibrinogenemia, an HLH-2004 criterion and a sign of impending bleeding/DIC in IVLBCL.
Demonstration of hemophagocytosis in marrow/spleen/liver supports HLH-2004 criteria; diagnostically critical in Asian variant.
Marrow infiltration plus HLH-mediated cytopenia suppression produces normocytic anemia in nearly all symptomatic IVLBCL.
Thrombocytopenia is common, especially with HLH overlap; also driven by consumption in DIC.
Leukopenia (esp. lymphopenia) is frequent in HLH-overlap IVLBCL; a tri-lineage cytopenia pattern alongside fever should prompt workup.
Hepatic sinusoidal infiltration produces transaminitis, often modest but persistent.
AST elevation parallels ALT and reflects hepatic involvement plus tissue ischemia.
Cholestatic-pattern liver enzyme elevation is common with hepatic IVLBCL infiltration.
Hyperbilirubinemia from sinusoidal infiltration and hemolysis (HLH overlap) contributes to jaundice.
Palpable hepatomegaly is a classical Asian-variant feature.
Splenomegaly is a frequent Asian-variant finding; absence does not exclude disease.
Negative finding: clinically apparent lymphadenopathy is conspicuously absent in IVLBCL—an important discriminator from nodal DLBCL and a reason why diagnosis is delayed.
Persistent or relapsing fever, often >38.5°C without source, is the dominant presenting complaint and a leading cause for the FUO workup that uncovers IVLBCL.
Drenching night sweats are part of the B-symptom complex.
Unintentional weight loss >10% body weight is common; reflects cytokine-driven cachexia.
Profound fatigue from cytokines plus anemia is near-universal.
IL-6–driven CRP elevation is typical and contributes to the FUO/sepsis-mimic presentation.
Markedly elevated ESR is common in IVLBCL.
Inflammation-driven negative acute-phase response and chronic illness produce hypoalbuminemia.
Encephalopathy, confusion, and rapidly progressive cognitive decline are classical CNS-IVLBCL findings often misattributed to dementia or delirium.
Multifocal stroke-like deficits, gait disturbance, cranial neuropathies, and myelopathy reflect microvascular CNS involvement.
Recurrent small-vessel infarcts produce TIA/stroke-like presentations in cryptogenic stroke workups; MRI typically shows multifocal punctate DWI lesions.
Seizures occur in a subset, reflecting cortical microinfarcts/inflammation.
Subacute headache is a frequent prodromal complaint with CNS involvement.
IVLBCL is a recognized cause of cryptogenic embolic-pattern stroke and multifocal small-vessel ischemia in older patients.
Without HD-MTX-based CNS prophylaxis, CNS relapse risk approaches 25–40%; this drives the routine integration of HD-MTX into modern IVLBCL regimens.

Erythematous patches/plaques, telangiectasia-like changes, painful nodules, and peau d'orange (especially on lower extremities/abdomen/breast) define cutaneous involvement and are the highest-yield biopsy target.
Microvascular alveolar capillary plugging produces progressive hypoxemia, often disproportionate to chest imaging.
Tachypnea accompanies hypoxemia and pulmonary diffusion impairment.
HRCT may show ground-glass opacities, reticular changes, mosaic perfusion; PET typically shows diffuse uptake; findings often subtle relative to hypoxemia severity.
Diffuse pulmonary microvascular obstruction can progress to ARDS-like respiratory failure.
Glomerular and peritubular involvement produces AKI; rises out of proportion to volume status are typical.
Subnephrotic to nephrotic-range proteinuria can occur with renal IVLBCL.
Renal IVLBCL plus tumor lysis plus contrast/medication exposure stack risk for AKI requiring dialysis.
Primary adrenal insufficiency from bilateral adrenal infiltration produces hyponatremia, often the first laboratory clue.
Mineralocorticoid deficiency produces hyperkalemia in established adrenal insufficiency.
Glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid deficiency reduces vascular tone and volume, producing orthostatic and refractory hypotension.
Latent adrenal insufficiency from infiltration unmasks as adrenal crisis with stressors—a recognized terminal event in undiagnosed IVLBCL.
Lymphoma-associated HLH is a leading early mortality driver in Asian-variant IVLBCL and warrants HLH-directed therapy alongside chemoimmunotherapy.
Hyperinflammatory state and consumption produce overt DIC with bleeding and thrombosis.
Intravascular tumor plus inflammation/coagulation activation increases venous and arterial thrombotic risk.
Cell turnover releases purines metabolized to urate within 24–72 h of induction.
Intracellular potassium release produces life-threatening hyperkalemia post-induction.
Calcium phosphate precipitation lowers ionized calcium, predisposing to tetany/arrhythmia.
Urate/phosphate nephropathy produces AKI; rasburicase plus hydration mitigates.
The interval between symptom onset and diagnosis (often months) accumulates ischemic and inflammatory organ damage that worsens prognosis even after appropriate therapy.

Random skin biopsy from clinically uninvolved skin (multiple sites including thigh/abdomen) is a uniquely high-yield (~50–80% sensitivity in suspected cases) diagnostic test that exploits dermal microvasculature involvement even without visible rash.
Bone marrow biopsy with CD20 immunostaining is the highest-yield diagnostic in Asian variant; intrasinusoidal CD20+ large cells are characteristic.
FDG-PET typically shows diffuse, multiorgan, non-mass-forming uptake (bone marrow, spleen, adrenals, lungs, kidneys) without dominant nodal disease—a relatively specific imaging signature.
Tumor cells uniformly express CD20/CD79a; this is therapeutically critical because rituximab efficacy depends on CD20 positivity.
Lymphoma cytokine activity produces recurrent or persistent fever over weeks to months.
Fever and inflammatory markers persist when the driver is lymphoma biology rather than ordinary bacterial infection.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Most prominent with pulmonary IVLBCL, mediastinal bulky disease, pleural/pericardial involvement, or severe anemia.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pulmonary capillary lymphoma produces exertional dyspnea and hypoxemia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: More likely with airway/mediastinal compression or pulmonary infiltration.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Diffuse interstitial or ground-glass pulmonary involvement can produce dry cough.
Pure lymphoma fever does not produce bacterial bloodstream growth, although secondary infection can override this.
Defective homing/extravasation keeps malignant cells intravascular and prevents ordinary nodal mass formation.
Absence of clinically apparent lymphadenopathy is a classic IVLBCL clue.
Intravascular lymphoma can involve brain, lung, kidney, liver, spleen, marrow, skin, and adrenal vessels without a dominant mass.
Patchy organ dysfunction from microvascular occlusion creates the occult multisystem pattern.
FUO or pulmonary IVLBCL is frequently treated as infection before tissue diagnosis, with no true antibacterial response.

axes.shape_free_text: Without treatment, mortality hazard rises rapidly over weeks to months (median untreated survival historically <12 months from symptom onset, often weeks once HLH-overlap or multi-organ failure declares). With R-CHOP + HD-MTX, hazard drops markedly after cycle 2; long-term survival 60–80% in fit limited-stage and 30–60% in HLH-variant cohorts. Adrenal crisis, ARDS, DIC, ischemic stroke, MAS-HLH are leading early hazards.
axes.second_peak: Late CNS relapse (6–24 months) without HD-MTX prophylaxis

axes.shape_free_text: Categorical phenotype indicator for hemophagocytic/Asian variant (BM, hepatosplenic, HLH-overlap dominance) versus classical Western variant (CNS, cutaneous predominance). Stable from disease onset.
Stable categorical: nearly all IVLBCL is CD20+. Required for rituximab benefit; rare CD20− cases require alternative regimens.
Pre-treatment random skin biopsy (multiple sites of clinically uninvolved skin) sensitivity 0.5–0.8 in suspected IVLBCL.
Bone marrow biopsy positivity (intrasinusoidal CD20+ large cells); sensitivity higher in Asian variant (~0.6–0.9) than classical variant.
Diffuse non-mass-forming FDG uptake (BM, spleen, adrenals, lungs, kidneys) without dominant nodal disease. Useful when high suspicion but no mass.
Subtle ground-glass opacities, mosaic perfusion, reticular changes; often disproportionately mild relative to hypoxemia severity.
Hazard rises 3–24 months after systemic CR if CNS prophylaxis not given; markedly reduced with HD-MTX integration.
Elevated to 3–10 mg/L commonly; correlates with tumor burden and prognosis.
Persistent or quotidian fever 38–40°C, often the longest-running prodrome.
axes.second_peak: May recur with relapse or HLH flare

axes.shape_free_text: Tachycardia from fever, anemia, hypoxemia, hypotension.
Tachypnea with pulmonary involvement.
Progressive desaturation from microvascular pulmonary involvement; often precedes radiographic findings.
Hypotension from adrenal insufficiency, sepsis-mimic cytokine storm, or HLH; often refractory until steroid replacement.
Normocytic anemia near-universal (often 7–10 g/dL); hemolysis component if HLH overlap.
Thrombocytopenia common in Asian/HLH variant; often <100, can be <20 in DIC.
Variable; often leukopenic in HLH overlap, sometimes leukocytosis with stress; classical absence of circulating tumor cells (rare lymphocyte morphology change).
Lymphopenia is common; low ALC has prognostic implications.
Markedly elevated (often 500–3000 U/L), one of the strongest IVLBCL signals; rises with relapse.
Ratios of 2–10 typical at diagnosis; component of IPI.
Markedly elevated (frequently 5,000–50,000 U/mL); especially high with HLH overlap; widely used in Japan as IVLBCL biomarker.
Markedly elevated (often >2,000–10,000) in HLH-overlap Asian variant.
Hypertriglyceridemia (often >265–500 mg/dL) in HLH-overlap.
Hypofibrinogenemia in HLH/DIC (<150 mg/dL is HLH-2004 criterion).
Persistent elevation (often 50–200 mg/L) reflecting IL-6 axis.
Markedly elevated (often >80 mm/hr).
Hypoalbuminemia (often 2.0–3.0 g/dL) from inflammation/cachexia.
Mild–moderate elevation (often 50–300 U/L) with hepatic involvement.
Parallel rise with ALT, often higher with ischemic component.
Cholestatic elevation common in hepatic IVLBCL.
Variable elevation; combined cholestatic and hemolytic component.
Rises with renal involvement and tumor lysis; often in 1.5–3.5 range, can require RRT.
Subnephrotic to occasional nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Baseline often modestly elevated (high tumor turnover); spikes 24–72 h post-induction with tumor lysis if not pretreated.
Two competing drivers: adrenal insufficiency (high) and chemotherapy-induced tumor lysis (high). Hyperkalemia is the most clinically relevant deviation.
Hyponatremia from primary AI ± SIADH-like cytokine effect; often the first lab clue.
Hypocalcemia post-tumor lysis from calcium phosphate precipitation.
Hypoglycemia possible with adrenal insufficiency and hepatic involvement.
Erythematous patches/plaques, telangiectasia-like changes, painful indurated nodules, peau d'orange (lower extremities/abdomen/breast). Predominant in cutaneous variant.
Subacute confusion, encephalopathy, rapidly progressive cognitive decline (months); a red flag in elderly with elevated LDH.
Multifocal deficits (motor, sensory, cranial nerve, gait); often progressive without treatment.
Recurrent TIA/stroke-like episodes, often over weeks; multifocal punctate DWI lesions on MRI.
Focal or generalized seizures from cortical microinfarcts/inflammation in subset.
Subacute persistent headache, often as prodrome.
Severe, near-universal; often the longest-standing symptom.
Drenching night sweats; B-symptom.
0.3–1 kg/week typical; >10% body weight over 6 months meets B-symptom criteria.
Palpable hepatomegaly, predominantly Asian variant.
Common in Asian variant.
Characteristically absent or minimal—a key discriminator from nodal DLBCL.
Hemophagocytic histiocytes seen on marrow aspirate in HLH-overlap.
Aggregate tumor burden surrogate; rises from diagnosis through pre-treatment, falls after R-CHOP cycles.
Accumulated multi-organ ischemic and inflammatory damage during diagnostic delay.
Peaks 1–5 days after induction.
Rises with progression of pulmonary involvement.
Rises with renal infiltration, tumor lysis, contrast/medication nephrotoxicity.
Rises with bilateral adrenal infiltration, peri-stress; mitigated by stress-dose steroids.
Hazard high in Asian variant; major early-mortality driver.
Rises with HLH overlap and severe disease.
Cumulative risk during active disease; falls with effective induction.
VTE risk increased; falls after induction.
Rises during chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (typically nadir day 7–14 each cycle).
Cyclical with chemotherapy nadirs.
Critical risk modifier with rituximab; baseline depends on HBsAg/anti-HBc status.
Required context: this axis is essentially 1 once IVLBCL diagnosis confirmed; affects HLH-treatment selection (etoposide-containing vs steroid-only).
Modifies HD-MTX feasibility and dosing.
Modifies anthracycline/HD-MTX dosing.
History-level fever burden over days to months, distinct from a single measured body temperature.

axes.display_name: Lack of clinical response to standard antibacterial therapy
axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever, inflammation, or organ findings despite antibacterial therapy that should have covered ordinary bacterial infection.
Patient-reported or observed breathlessness from pulmonary, cardiac, mediastinal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement.
Dry or productive cough as a symptom axis; mechanism depends on pulmonary, airway, cardiac, or mediastinal involvement.
Probability that standard blood cultures grow a causative bacterium; expected to remain low in uncomplicated lymphoma fever.
Clinically significant lymph-node enlargement; typically absent or minimal in IVLBCL despite systemic disease.
Fever with neurologic, pulmonary, renal, hepatic, marrow, or adrenal dysfunction out of proportion to nodal or mass lesions.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: LDH and tumor burden track together at diagnosis and through response monitoring; residual covariance beyond direct mechanism edge.
Both biomarkers follow tumor activity and HLH biology; commonly co-elevated in IVLBCL.
Both are HLH-2004 criteria driven by macrophage activation.
Inverse relationship is classical in HLH (rising ferritin, falling fibrinogen).
Hyponatremia and hypotension co-occur from adrenal insufficiency; their co-presentation should prompt cosyntropin testing.
Both rise simultaneously in tumor lysis syndrome.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rituximab targets CD20; absent expression abolishes benefit.
Rituximab can precipitate fatal HBV reactivation in HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+; antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir/tenofovir) required.

failure_modes: rare hyperprogression on initiation when high tumor burden
incomplete coverage of CNS sanctuary requiring HD-MTX adjunct

side_effects.interpretation: Hypogammaglobulinemia and B-cell depletion increase infection risk for months.
Risk of HBV reactivation in seropositive patients.
Infusion-related cytokine release reaction (especially first dose).

treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone of R-CHOP; integral to all modern IVLBCL induction; contributed measurable improvement over CHOP-alone in IVLBCL series.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxorubicin and vincristine require dose adjustment in hepatic dysfunction.
Cyclophosphamide metabolite clearance; supportive care intensification needed.

failure_modes: early death from MAS-HLH or multi-organ failure before adequate cycles delivered
cardiotoxicity in elderly limiting full anthracycline dose
isolated CNS relapse if no HD-MTX prophylaxis added

side_effects.interpretation: Profound neutropenia at days 7–14 of each cycle.

treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone induction for IVLBCL across both variants; typically 6–8 cycles ± HD-MTX integration for CNS coverage.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: HD-MTX clearance is renal; impairment causes severe toxicity unless dose-adjusted with leucovorin rescue and glucarpidase availability.

failure_modes: delayed MTX clearance with mucositis, AKI, myelosuppression
incomplete CNS coverage without intrathecal supplement

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity from precipitation in tubules.

treatments.context_specific_role: Integrated with R-CHOP (e.g., R-CHOP/HD-MTX every 21 days, or interpolated cycles) to address sanctuary CNS disease and prevent CNS relapse — the most clinically meaningful improvement in IVLBCL outcomes after rituximab.

failure_modes: limited tissue penetration beyond CSF surfaces
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative or adjunct CNS prophylaxis when HD-MTX not feasible (renal failure, frailty); inferior to systemic HD-MTX for parenchymal coverage.
Considered for fit younger patients in first remission, particularly with HLH variant or high-IPI disease, given relapse risk after R-CHOP/HD-MTX.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hydrogen peroxide byproduct causes severe hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

treatments.context_specific_role: Primary prophylaxis for high tumor-burden IVLBCL undergoing R-CHOP induction; dramatically reduces TLS-AKI hazard.
Lower-intensity TLS prophylaxis when tumor burden moderate; usually combined with hydration.

side_effects.interpretation: Volume overload may worsen oxygenation in pulmonary IVLBCL.

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard pre-/peri-induction support for TLS prophylaxis and AKI prevention.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adrenal insufficiency from bilateral adrenal infiltration requires lifelong replacement; missed diagnosis is a recognized cause of refractory shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Required when adrenal involvement causes AI; given physiologically (not as anti-tumor steroid) and stress-dosed during chemotherapy/illness.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Etoposide reduces activated T-cell/macrophage burden in HLH; benefit limited to HLH-overlap or HLH-directed protocols.

failure_modes: marrow exhaustion in already cytopenic HLH patient
treatments.context_specific_role: Used in HLH-2004-style regimens or DA-EPOCH-R-type protocols for IVLBCL with secondary HLH; addresses HLH biology in parallel with anti-lymphoma therapy.
Routine PCP prophylaxis during R-CHOP and rituximab-containing therapy due to prolonged B-cell and CD4 depletion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: All HBsAg+ and most anti-HBc+ patients receiving rituximab require entecavir or tenofovir prophylaxis to prevent fatal reactivation.

side_effects.interpretation: Tenofovir nephrotoxicity risk; entecavir preferred in CKD.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mandatory for HBV-exposed patients receiving rituximab-based therapy; continued ≥12 months after completion.
Reduces febrile neutropenia hazard during R-CHOP/HD-MTX, especially in elderly or after FN history.
Salvage option in relapsed/refractory IVLBCL or unfit patients; CNS-permeable and active in some refractory cohorts.

elderly_60_to_85.trajectory_modulation: Median age at diagnosis ~60–70 years; nearly all cases >50.

very_elderly_over_80.trajectory_modulation: Reduced fitness limits R-CHOP intensity and HD-MTX feasibility, worsening outcomes.

young_under_40.trajectory_modulation: IVLBCL exceedingly rare under 40; consider in unexplained FUO + high LDH but with caution.

asian.trajectory_modulation: Strongly biased toward Asian variant phenotype: BM, hepatosplenic, HLH-overlap predominant; less CNS/cutaneous predominance at presentation.

non_asian.trajectory_modulation: Classical/Western phenotype with CNS and cutaneous predominance.

female_with_skin_only_lesions.trajectory_modulation: Cutaneous variant has female predominance and substantially better prognosis when skin-limited at diagnosis.

present.trajectory_modulation: Modestly increased risk; not a strong risk factor unlike EBV-driven lymphomas.

supportive_care: Prompt random skin biopsy from clinically uninvolved skin (multiple sites including thigh/abdomen/breast) and bone marrow biopsy with CD20 immunostaining when IVLBCL suspected — diagnostic delay is the dominant modifiable prognostic factor.
Aggressive tumor lysis prophylaxis (rasburicase if high burden, allopurinol otherwise, isotonic IV hydration, urine output ≥2 mL/kg/hr) before first R-CHOP cycle.

Cosyntropin stimulation testing in any patient with bilateral adrenal enlargement or unexplained hyponatremia/hypotension; initiate hydrocortisone replacement preemptively if AI confirmed and stress-dose during chemotherapy.
HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) before rituximab, with entecavir or tenofovir prophylaxis for HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+ patients, continued ≥12 months after rituximab completion.
PCP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) and consider antifungal/HSV prophylaxis during treatment given prolonged B-cell and CD4 depletion.
G-CSF primary prophylaxis in elderly or after febrile neutropenia event.
Echocardiogram before anthracycline initiation; surveillance LVEF in cumulative-dose patients.
Baseline brain MRI and lumbar puncture (CSF cytology + flow cytometry) at diagnosis given high CNS involvement rate; integrate HD-MTX with R-CHOP for CNS prophylaxis when feasible.
Monitor LDH, sIL-2R, ferritin, CRP, fibrinogen serially as response and HLH-flare biomarkers.
VTE prophylaxis during hospitalization; balance against thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk in HLH overlap.

Multidisciplinary supportive care including psychiatry/neurology for CNS variant, dermatology for cutaneous variant biopsies, and palliative care for elderly with diagnostic delay-related multi-organ injury.
Family counseling regarding diagnosis, prognosis (better in cutaneous-only variant, worse with HLH overlap), and treatment toxicity, particularly for elderly patients.
